common_name: Tim Herrington Daylily (2023 Stout Medal Copper-Red Double Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; heavy branching and high bud count reward regular deadheading.

directions: Hybridized by Scott Elliott and named for noted Region 5 hybridizer Tim Herrington, this small double-form daylily won the AHS Stout Silver Medal in 2023 for its compact copper-red blooms marked with a distinct golden-yellow midrib on each petal. Heavily branched scapes carry a high bud count that extends the bloom season well beyond most cultivars, and the double ruffled form holds up cleanly through summer heat. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil with consistent moisture, and divide crowded clumps every few years to keep bud counts high.

common_name: Ed Brown Daylily (2006 Stout Medal Pink Gold-Edged Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; strong rebloom benefits from a mid-season feeding.

directions: Hybridized by Salter and awarded the Stout Silver Medal in 2006, Ed Brown produces large, softly ruffled pale-pink blooms with a faint gold blush at the center and a distinct golden picotee edge. Semi-evergreen tetraploid foliage supports strong branching scapes and dependable rebloom through the growing season in warmer climates. Plant in enriched, well-drained soil and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Green Glitter Daylily (1977 Stout Medal Pale Yellow Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; semi-evergreen foliage may need winter protection in cold zones.

directions: Hybridized by D.J. Harrison and honored with the Stout Silver Medal in 1977, Green Glitter carries a pale lemon-yellow self bloom set above a glowing chartreuse throat. Diploid clumps bloom in early-to-mid season and can throw a light scattering of late-season rebloom under good conditions. Grow in well-drained soil with regular moisture and divide clumps every three to four years to renew flowering vigor.

common_name: Winning Ways Daylily (1974 Stout Medal Greenish-Yellow Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Winner of the AHS Stout Silver Medal in 1974, Winning Ways is prized for its unusual flat, crisply colored greenish-yellow blooms centered on a small green heart. Wide, overlapping petals give the flower excellent substance, while gently twirled sepals add distinctive form. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and divide clumps every few years to sustain heavy flowering.

common_name: Luxury Lace Daylily (1965 Stout Medal Pale Lavender-Pink Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil; bloom color shifts warmer in full sun and cooler in partial shade.

directions: Introduced by Spalding and awarded the Stout Silver Medal in 1965, Luxury Lace bears bell-shaped, pale lavender-pink blooms with a soft yellow-green throat. Flower tone is sensitive to light exposure, taking on a warmer salmon cast in full sun and a cooler lavender hue in lighter shade. Dormant clumps perform reliably in a wide range of climates; plant in well-drained soil and divide every few years as clumps thicken.

common_name: Cartwheels Daylily (1966 Stout Medal Deep Yellow Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Bred by Fay-Russell from a cross of Soledad and Signal Light, Cartwheels earned the Stout Silver Medal in 1966 for its clear, deep yellow self blooms of excellent round form. This dormant diploid flowers in mid-to-late season and forms dense, vigorous clumps over time. Grow in well-drained soil in full sun and divide every three to four years to keep the display floriferous.

common_name: Prima Donna Daylily (1955 Stout Medal Rosy Orange Polychrome Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; a tall heirloom well suited to the back of a mixed border.

directions: Introduced in 1946 and later recognized with the Stout Silver Medal in 1955, Prima Donna carries a light rosy-orange polychrome bloom that blends several warm tones across each petal. Tall, sturdy scapes hold the flowers well above the dormant foliage, making it a good choice for the middle or back of a perennial bed. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Renee Daylily (1971 Stout Medal Light Yellow Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Hybridized by Dill and awarded the AHS Stout Silver Medal in 1971, Renee bears clear light-yellow blooms brightened by a soft green throat. This dormant diploid forms compact, dependable clumps and blooms freely over a long midsummer season. Grow in well-drained soil with consistent moisture and divide every few years to keep flowering strong.

common_name: Sabie Daylily (1983 Stout Medal Golden Yellow Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; evergreen foliage benefits from winter mulch in colder zones.

directions: Hybridized by MacMillan and honored with the Stout Silver Medal in 1983, Sabie produces a clean golden-yellow self bloom with a soft green throat on a compact, early-flowering plant. The small evergreen diploid clump stays tidy in the border and blooms reliably each season with minimal care. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and divide every few years to keep the clump vigorous.
